rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: If \(x = ab^3\) and \(y = a^3b\), where a and b are prime numbers, then \([\text{HCF}(x, y) - \text{LCM}(x, y)]\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
\(x = ab^3\) and \(y = a^3b\) with a and b prime, so HCF\((x, y) = ab\) and LCM\((x, y) = a^3b^3\).

HCF \(-\) LCM \(= ab - a^3b^3 = ab(1 - a^2b^2) = ab(1 - ab)(1 + ab)\).

This is option (D) \(ab(1 - ab)(1 + ab)\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: \(\left(1 + \sqrt{3}\right)^2 - \left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right)^2\) is :
rows.solution:
\((1 + \sqrt{3})^2 - (1 - \sqrt{3})^2 = (4 + 2\sqrt{3}) - (4 - 2\sqrt{3}) = 4\sqrt{3}\).

\(4\sqrt{3}\) is positive and irrational, which is option (C) a positive irrational number.

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: The value of ‘a’ for which \(ax^2 + x + a = 0\) has equal and positive roots is :
rows.solution:
Equal roots need the discriminant to be zero: \(1 - 4a^2 = 0\), so \(a = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}\).

The equal root is \(-\dfrac{1}{2a}\). For \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}\) it is \(-1\); for \(a = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) it is \(1\), which is positive.

So \(a = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), which is option (D) \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

rows.stem: The distance of a point A from x-axis is 3 units. Which of the following cannot be coordinates of the point A ?
rows.solution:
The distance from the x-axis is the absolute value of the y-coordinate, so A must have \(y = \pm 3\).

\((3, 1)\) has \(y = 1\), so it is 1 unit from the x-axis. This is option (D) \((3, 1)\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: The number of red balls in a bag is 10 more than the number of black balls. If the probability of drawing a red ball at random from this bag is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\), then the total number of balls in the bag is :
rows.solution:
Let there be \(x\) black balls. Then there are \(x + 10\) red balls and \(2x + 10\) balls in all.

\(\dfrac{x + 10}{2x + 10} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(5x + 50 = 6x + 30\) and \(x = 20\).

Total \(= 2(20) + 10 = 50\), which is option (A) \(50\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The value of ‘p’ for which the equations \(px + 3y = p - 3\), \(12x + py = p\) has infinitely many solutions is :
rows.solution:
Write the equations as \(px + 3y - (p - 3) = 0\) and \(12x + py - p = 0\). Infinitely many solutions need

\(\dfrac{p}{12} = \dfrac{3}{p} = \dfrac{p - 3}{p}\).

\(\dfrac{p}{12} = \dfrac{3}{p}\) gives \(p^2 = 36\), so \(p = \pm 6\). \(\dfrac{3}{p} = \dfrac{p - 3}{p}\) gives \(p - 3 = 3\), so \(p = 6\).

Only \(p = 6\) satisfies both, which is option (B) \(6\) only.

rows.stem: \(\Delta ABC\) and \(\Delta PQR\) are shown in the adjoining figures. The measure of \(\angle C\) is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - every measurement (AB 3.8 cm, AC 3√3 cm, BC 6 cm; QR 7.6 cm, PR 6√3 cm, PQ 12 cm, angles 80 degrees at R and 60 degrees at Q) is given only in the drawing. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
In the figures, \(AB = 3.8\), \(BC = 6\), \(CA = 3\sqrt{3}\) cm and \(RQ = 7.6\), \(QP = 12\), \(PR = 6\sqrt{3}\) cm.

\(\dfrac{AB}{RQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QP} = \dfrac{CA}{PR} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta RQP\) (SSS), with \(C \leftrightarrow P\).

\(\angle C = \angle P = 180^\circ - 80^\circ - 60^\circ = 40^\circ\), which is option (D) \(40^\circ\).

rows.stem: \(\tan 2A = 3\tan A\) is true, when the measure of \(\angle A\) is :
rows.solution:
At \(A = 30^\circ\): \(\tan 2A = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\) and \(3\tan 30^\circ = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}\). They are equal.

(At \(45^\circ\), \(\tan 90^\circ\) is not defined; at \(60^\circ\), \(\tan 120^\circ = -\sqrt{3} \neq 3\sqrt{3}\); at \(90^\circ\), \(\tan A\) is not defined.)

This is option (D) \(30^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
rows.stem: Which of the following statements is true ?
rows.solution:
Between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), \(\cos\theta\) decreases as \(\theta\) increases, so \(\cos 20^\circ > \cos 70^\circ\).

The others are false: \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) increase, so \(\sin 20^\circ < \sin 70^\circ\) and \(\tan 20^\circ < \tan 70^\circ\); and \(\sin 20^\circ = \cos 70^\circ < \cos 20^\circ\).

This is option (C) \(\cos 20^\circ > \cos 70^\circ\).

rows.stem: A 30 m long rope is tightly stretched and tied from the top of pole to the ground. If the rope makes an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the ground, the height of the pole is :
rows.solution:
The rope is the hypotenuse, making \(60^\circ\) with the ground, so the height is

\(h = 30\sin 60^\circ = 30 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 15\sqrt{3}\) m. This is option (D) \(15\sqrt{3}\) m.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: On the top face of the wooden cube of side 7 cm, hemispherical depressions of radius 0.35 cm are to be formed by taking out the wood. The maximum number of depressions that can be formed is :
rows.solution:
Each depression has diameter \(2 \times 0.35 = 0.7\) cm. Along each 7 cm edge of the face, \(\dfrac{7}{0.7} = 10\) depressions fit.

The maximum number is \(10 \times 10 = 100\), which is option (B) \(100\).

rows.stem: The cumulative frequency for calculating median is obtained by adding the frequencies of all the :

options.label: A
options.text: classes up to the median class

rows.solution:
In the median formula \(l + \dfrac{\frac{n}{2} - cf}{f} \times h\), \(cf\) is the cumulative frequency of the class before the median class, that is, the sum of the frequencies of all the classes preceding it.

This is option (C) classes preceding the median class.

rows.stem: If mean and median of given set of observations are 10 and 11 respectively, then the value of mode is :
In the adjoining figure, AB is the chord of the larger circle touching the smaller circle. The centre of both the circles is O. If AB = 2r and OP = r, then the radius of larger circle is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the point P (where the chord AB touches the smaller circle, with OP drawn) is named only in the drawing of the two concentric circles. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The chord AB touches the smaller circle at P, so \(OP \perp AB\), and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord: \(AP = r\).

In right triangle OPA, \(OA^2 = OP^2 + AP^2 = r^2 + r^2 = 2r^2\), so \(OA = \sqrt{2}\,r\).

This is option (D) \(\sqrt{2}\,r\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: A parallelogram having one of its sides 5 cm circumscribes a circle. The perimeter of parallelogram is :

options.label: C
options.text: more than 20 cm but less than 40 cm

rows.solution:
Tangents from an external point are equal, so for a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, \(AB + CD = AD + BC\). In a parallelogram this gives \(2AB = 2AD\), so all four sides are equal: it is a rhombus.

The perimeter is \(4 \times 5 = 20\) cm, which is option (A) 20 cm.

rows.stem: E and F are points on the sides AB and AC respectively of a \(\Delta ABC\) such that \(\dfrac{AE}{EB} = \dfrac{AF}{FC} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Which of the following relation is true ?
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{AE}{EB} = \dfrac{AF}{FC}\), so by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(EF \parallel BC\), and \(\Delta AEF \sim \Delta ABC\).

\(\dfrac{AE}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{EF}{BC} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(BC = 3EF\).

This is option (D) BC = 3EF.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Which of the following statements is true for a polynomial p(x) of degree 3?

options.label: A
options.text: p(x) has at most two distinct zeroes.

options.label: B
options.text: p(x) has at least two distinct zeroes.

options.label: C
options.text: p(x) has exactly three distinct zeroes.

options.label: D
options.text: p(x) has at most three distinct zeroes.

rows.solution:
A polynomial of degree 3 has at most 3 zeroes. It may have fewer distinct zeroes: \(x^3\) has only one, and \(x^3 + x\) has only one real zero.

This is option (D) p(x) has at most three distinct zeroes.

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: A pair of dice is thrown. The probability that sum of numbers appearing on top faces is at most 10 is :
rows.solution:
There are 36 equally likely outcomes. A sum greater than 10 is 11 or 12: \((5, 6), (6, 5), (6, 6)\), which is 3 outcomes.

\(P(\text{sum} \leq 10) = 1 - \dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{11}{12}\), which is option (D) \(\dfrac{11}{12}\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** \(4^n\) ends with digit 0 for some natural number n.

**Reason (R) :** For a number ‘x’ having 2 and 5 as its prime factors, \(x^n\) always ends with digit 0 for every natural number n.
rows.context: In question number 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option :

options.label: A
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
\(4^n = 2^{2n}\) has only the prime 2. A number ending in 0 is divisible by 10, so it needs 5 as a prime factor. \(4^n\) never ends in 0, and the Assertion is false.

If x has 2 and 5 as prime factors, x is a multiple of 10, so \(x^n\) is a multiple of 10 and ends in 0. The Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Tangents drawn at the end points of a diameter of a circle are always parallel to each other.

**Reason (R) :** The lengths of tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle are always equal.
rows.context: In question number 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Choose the correct option :

options.label: A
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The tangents at the ends of a diameter are both perpendicular to that diameter, so they are parallel. The Assertion is true.

Tangents from an external point to a circle are equal in length. The Reason is true.

But equal tangent lengths say nothing about the tangents at the ends of a diameter being parallel, so the Reason does not explain the Assertion. This is option (B).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem:
Solve the following system of equations algebraically :

\(30x + 44y = 10\) ; \(40x + 55y = 13\)
rows.solution:
Multiply the first equation by 4 and the second by 3:

\(120x + 176y = 40\) ... (1)

\(120x + 165y = 39\) ... (2)

Subtracting (2) from (1): \(11y = 1\), so \(y = \dfrac{1}{11}\).

Substituting in \(30x + 44y = 10\): \(30x + 4 = 10\), so \(x = \dfrac{1}{5}\).

\(x = \dfrac{1}{5}\), \(y = \dfrac{1}{11}\).

rows.stem: A 1.5 m tall boy is walking away from the base of a lamp post which is 12 m high, at the speed of 2.5 m/sec. Find the length of his shadow after 3 seconds.
rows.solution:
Let AB be the lamp post (12 m) and CD the boy (1.5 m), standing at D. The light from A over the top of the boy's head C meets the ground at E, so DE is the shadow. Let \(DE = x\) m.

In 3 seconds the boy walks \(2.5 \times 3 = 7.5\) m, so \(BD = 7.5\) m and \(BE = 7.5 + x\).

\(AB \parallel CD\) (both vertical), so \(\Delta ABE \sim \Delta CDE\) (AA) and \(\dfrac{CD}{AB} = \dfrac{DE}{BE}\):

\(\dfrac{1.5}{12} = \dfrac{x}{7.5 + x}\), so \(12x = 11.25 + 1.5x\) and \(x = \dfrac{11.25}{10.5} = \dfrac{15}{14}\).

The shadow is \(\dfrac{15}{14}\) m, about 1.07 m, long.

rows.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, side AD is produced to a point E and BE intersects CD at F. Prove that \(\Delta ABE \sim \Delta CFB\)
rows.solution:
In triangles ABE and CFB:

\(\angle A = \angle C\) (opposite angles of a parallelogram).

\(AE \parallel BC\) (AD is produced to E, and \(AD \parallel BC\)), and BE is a transversal, so \(\angle AEB = \angle CBF\) (alternate angles).

So \(\Delta ABE \sim \Delta CFB\) (AA similarity).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Find the coordinates of the point C which lies on the line AB produced such that AC = 2BC, where coordinates of points A and B are \((-1, 7)\) and \((4, -3)\) respectively.
rows.solution:
C lies on AB produced with \(AC = 2BC\), so \(AB = AC - BC = BC\): B is the mid-point of AC.

Let \(C = (x, y)\). Then \(\dfrac{-1 + x}{2} = 4\), so \(x = 9\), and \(\dfrac{7 + y}{2} = -3\), so \(y = -13\).

The coordinates of C are \((9, -13)\).

rows.stem: Find the value of x for which \((\sin A + \operatorname{cosec} A)^2 + (\cos A + \sec A)^2 = x + \tan^2 A + \cot^2 A\)
rows.solution:
Expand the left side:

\(\sin^2 A + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A + 2 + \cos^2 A + \sec^2 A + 2\)

\(= (\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A) + (1 + \cot^2 A) + (1 + \tan^2 A) + 4 = 7 + \tan^2 A + \cot^2 A\).

Comparing with \(x + \tan^2 A + \cot^2 A\): \(x = 7\).

rows.stem:
Evaluate the following :

\(\dfrac{3\sin 30^\circ - 4\sin^3 30^\circ}{2\sin^2 50^\circ + 2\cos^2 50^\circ}\)
rows.solution:
Numerator: \(3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} - 4 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\).

Denominator: \(2(\sin^2 50^\circ + \cos^2 50^\circ) = 2 \times 1 = 2\).

The value is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

rows.stem:
Two friends Anil and Ashraf were born in the December month in the year 2010. Find the probability that :

(i) they share same date of birth.

(ii) they have different dates of birth.
rows.solution:
December 2010 has 31 days, and each of Ashraf's 31 possible birth dates is taken as equally likely.

(i) \(P(\text{same date of birth}) = \dfrac{1}{31}\).

(ii) \(P(\text{different dates of birth}) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{31} = \dfrac{30}{31}\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational. Then \(\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}\), where p and q are integers, \(q \neq 0\), and p and q are coprime.

Squaring, \(p^2 = 2q^2\). So 2 divides \(p^2\), and since 2 is prime, 2 divides p ... (1)

Write \(p = 2a\). Then \(4a^2 = 2q^2\), so \(q^2 = 2a^2\). So 2 divides \(q^2\), and hence 2 divides q ... (2)

From (1) and (2), 2 divides both p and q, which contradicts p and q being coprime.

So the assumption is wrong, and \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Let x and y be two distinct prime numbers and \(p = x^2y^3\), \(q = xy^4\), \(r = x^5y^2\). Find the HCF and LCM of p, q and r. Further check if \(\text{HCF}(p, q, r) \times \text{LCM}(p, q, r) = p \times q \times r\) or not.
rows.solution:
\(p = x^2y^3\), \(q = xy^4\), \(r = x^5y^2\).

HCF takes the smallest power of each prime: HCF\((p, q, r) = x^1y^2 = xy^2\).

LCM takes the largest power: LCM\((p, q, r) = x^5y^4\).

HCF \(\times\) LCM \(= x^6y^6\), while \(p \times q \times r = x^{2+1+5}y^{3+4+2} = x^8y^9\).

So HCF\((p, q, r) \times\) LCM\((p, q, r) \neq p \times q \times r\). (The product rule holds for two numbers, not for three.)

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: The monthly incomes of two persons are in the ratio 9 : 7 and their monthly expenditures are in the ratio 4 : 3. If each saved ₹ 5,000, express the given situation algebraically as a system of linear equations in two variables. Hence, find their respective monthly incomes.
rows.solution:
Let the incomes be ₹\(9x\) and ₹\(7x\), and the expenditures ₹\(4y\) and ₹\(3y\). Each saves ₹5000:

\(9x - 4y = 5000\) ... (1)

\(7x - 3y = 5000\) ... (2)

Multiply (1) by 3 and (2) by 4: \(27x - 12y = 15000\) and \(28x - 12y = 20000\). Subtracting, \(x = 5000\), and then \(y = 10000\).

The monthly incomes are ₹45000 and ₹35000.

rows.stem: \(P(x, y)\), \(Q(-2, -3)\) and \(R(2, 3)\) are the vertices of a right triangle PQR right angled at P. Find the relationship between x and y. Hence, find all possible values of x for which y = 2.
Prove that \(\dfrac{\cos A + \sin A - 1}{\cos A - \sin A + 1} = \operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A\)
rows.solution:
Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(\sin A\):

LHS \(= \dfrac{\cot A + 1 - \operatorname{cosec} A}{\cot A - 1 + \operatorname{cosec} A}\).

Replace the 1 in the numerator by \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 A - \cot^2 A\):

\(= \dfrac{(\cot A - \operatorname{cosec} A) + (\operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A)(\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A)}{\cot A - 1 + \operatorname{cosec} A}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A)(\operatorname{cosec} A + \cot A - 1)}{\cot A - 1 + \operatorname{cosec} A} = \operatorname{cosec} A - \cot A =\) RHS.

rows.stem: If \(\cot\theta + \cos\theta = p\) and \(\cot\theta - \cos\theta = q\), prove that \(p^2 - q^2 = 4\sqrt{pq}\)
rows.solution:
LHS \(= p^2 - q^2 = (p + q)(p - q) = (2\cot\theta)(2\cos\theta) = 4\cot\theta\cos\theta\).

RHS \(= 4\sqrt{pq} = 4\sqrt{\cot^2\theta - \cos^2\theta} = 4\sqrt{\cos^2\theta\left(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - 1\right)} = 4\sqrt{\cos^2\theta\cot^2\theta} = 4\cot\theta\cos\theta\)

(taking \(\theta\) acute, so \(\cot\theta\cos\theta > 0\)). Hence LHS \(=\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are zeroes of a quadratic polynomial \(px^2 + qx + 1\). Form a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are \(\dfrac{2}{\alpha}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{\beta}\).
rows.solution:
For \(px^2 + qx + 1\): \(\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{q}{p}\) and \(\alpha\beta = \dfrac{1}{p}\).

Sum of the new zeroes: \(\dfrac{2}{\alpha} + \dfrac{2}{\beta} = \dfrac{2(\alpha + \beta)}{\alpha\beta} = 2\left(-\dfrac{q}{p}\right) \times p = -2q\).

Product: \(\dfrac{2}{\alpha} \times \dfrac{2}{\beta} = \dfrac{4}{\alpha\beta} = 4p\).

The polynomial is \(x^2 - (\text{sum})x + \text{product} = x^2 + 2qx + 4p\) (or any non-zero multiple of it).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: Rectangle ABCD circumscribes the circle of radius 10 cm. Prove that ABCD is a square. Hence, find the perimeter of ABCD.
rows.solution:
Let the circle touch AB, BC, CD and DA at P, Q, R and S. Tangents from an external point are equal:

\(AP = AS\), \(BP = BQ\), \(CR = CQ\), \(DR = DS\).

Adding: \((AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)\), so \(AB + CD = AD + BC\) ... (1)

ABCD is a rectangle, so \(AB = CD\) and \(BC = AD\). From (1), \(2AB = 2AD\), so \(AB = AD\): adjacent sides are equal, and ABCD is a square.

The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle, 20 cm, so the perimeter is \(4 \times 20 = 80\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: The sides of a right triangle are such that the longest side is 4 m more than the shortest side and the third side is 2 m less than the longest side. Find the length of each side of the triangle. Also, find the difference between the numerical values of the area and the perimeter of the given triangle.
rows.solution:
Let the shortest side be \(x\) m. Then the longest side (the hypotenuse) is \(x + 4\) m, and the third side is \(x + 2\) m.

\((x + 4)^2 = x^2 + (x + 2)^2\)

\(x^2 + 8x + 16 = 2x^2 + 4x + 4\), so \(x^2 - 4x - 12 = 0\) and \((x - 6)(x + 2) = 0\).

A length is positive, so \(x = 6\). The sides are 6 m, 8 m and 10 m.

Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24\) m\(^2\); perimeter \(= 6 + 8 + 10 = 24\) m.

The difference between the numerical values is \(24 - 24 = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: Express the equation \(\dfrac{x - 2}{x - 3} + \dfrac{x - 4}{x - 5} = \dfrac{10}{3}\) ; \((x \neq 3, 5)\) as a quadratic equation in standard form. Hence, find the roots of the equation so formed.

The corresponding sides of \(\Delta ABC\) and \(\Delta PQR\) are in the ratio 3 : 5. \(AD \perp BC\) and \(PS \perp QR\) as shown in the following figures :

(i) Prove that \(\Delta ADC \sim \Delta PSR\)

(ii) If AD = 4 cm, find the length of PS.

(iii) Using (ii) find ar \((\Delta ABC)\) : ar \((\Delta PQR)\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the two triangles with the altitudes AD and PS drawn; the stem states the ratio and both perpendiculars. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AC}{PR} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\) (SSS), and \(\angle C = \angle R\).

(i) In triangles ADC and PSR: \(\angle ADC = \angle PSR = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle C = \angle R\). So \(\Delta ADC \sim \Delta PSR\) (AA).

(ii) \(\dfrac{AD}{PS} = \dfrac{AC}{PR} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(\dfrac{4}{PS} = \dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(PS = \dfrac{20}{3}\) cm.

(iii) \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(\Delta ABC)}{\text{ar}(\Delta PQR)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \times BC \times AD}{\frac{1}{2} \times QR \times PS} = \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{9}{25}\).

ar\((\Delta ABC)\) : ar\((\Delta PQR) = 9 : 25\).

rows.stem:
State basic proportionality theorem. Use it to prove the following :

If three parallel lines l, m, n are intersected by transversals q and s as shown in the adjoining figure, then \(\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{DE}{EF}\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the points A, B, C (on transversal q) and D, E, F (on transversal s) where they cross l, m, n are named only in the drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Basic Proportionality Theorem: if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.

Join AF, meeting the line m at G.

In triangle ACF, \(BG \parallel CF\) (B and G are on m, C and F on n), so \(\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{AG}{GF}\) ... (1)

In triangle FDA, \(GE \parallel AD\) (G and E on m, A and D on l), so \(\dfrac{FE}{ED} = \dfrac{FG}{GA}\), that is \(\dfrac{DE}{EF} = \dfrac{AG}{GF}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \dfrac{DE}{EF}\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A wooden cubical die is formed by forming hemispherical depressions on each face of the cube such that face 1 has one depression, face 2 has two depressions and so on. The sum of number of hemispherical depressions on opposite faces is always 7. If the edge of the cubical die measures 5 cm and each hemispherical depression is of diameter 1.4 cm, find the total surface area of the die so formed.
rows.solution:
Opposite faces add to 7, so the faces carry 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 depressions: \(1 + 2 + \cdots + 6 = 21\) depressions in all.

Each depression removes a circle of radius \(r = 0.7\) cm from the face and adds a hemispherical surface of area \(2\pi r^2\).

TSA \(= 6 \times 5^2 + 21 \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (0.7)^2 - 21 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (0.7)^2\)

\(= 150 + 21 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.49 = 150 + 32.34 = 182.34\) cm\(^2\).

rows.context:

In order to spread awareness about Olympic games, students of Class-X took part in various activities organised by the school. One such group of students made 5 circular rings in the school lawn with the help of ropes. Each circular ring required 44 m of rope.

Also, in the shaded regions as shown in the figure, students made rangoli showcasing various sports and games. It is given that \(\Delta OAB\) is an equilateral triangle and all unshaded regions are congruent.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the five overlapping circles with the shaded and unshaded regions; this part needs only the 44 m stated in the passage. The coloured Olympic rings beside it are decorative. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Each ring needs 44 m of rope, which is its circumference:

\(2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r = 44\), so \(r = 7\) m.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - O (the centre of the first circle) and A, B (where it meets the second circle) are named only in the drawing. Page idx 12.

rows.stem: Find the area of shaded region \(R_1\).
rows.context:
The Olympic symbol comprising five interlocking rings represents the union of the five continents of the world and the meeting of athletes from all over the world at the Olympic games. In order to spread awareness about Olympic games, students of Class-X took part in various activities organised by the school. One such group of students made 5 circular rings in the school lawn with the help of ropes. Each circular ring required 44 m of rope.

Also, in the shaded regions as shown in the figure, students made rangoli showcasing various sports and games. It is given that \(\Delta OAB\) is an equilateral triangle and all unshaded regions are congruent.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the shaded region \(R_1\) (the first circle less its two unshaded lens-shaped overlaps) is defined only in the drawing. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
The unshaded region in the first ring is the overlap with the second ring. It is made of two congruent segments, each cut off by the chord AB with central angle \(60^\circ\) in a circle of radius 7 m.

Area of one segment \(= \dfrac{60}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 7^2 = \dfrac{77}{3} - \dfrac{49\sqrt{3}}{4}\).

Area of \(R_1\) \(=\) area of circle \(-\) 2 segments \(= 154 - 2\left(\dfrac{77}{3} - \dfrac{49\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = \left(\dfrac{308}{3} + \dfrac{49\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) m\(^2\)

\(\approx 102.67 + 42.44 = 145.1\) m\(^2\).

rows.stem: Find the length of rope around the unshaded regions.
rows.context:
The Olympic symbol comprising five interlocking rings represents the union of the five continents of the world and the meeting of athletes from all over the world at the Olympic games. In order to spread awareness about Olympic games, students of Class-X took part in various activities organised by the school. One such group of students made 5 circular rings in the school lawn with the help of ropes. Each circular ring required 44 m of rope.

Also, in the shaded regions as shown in the figure, students made rangoli showcasing various sports and games. It is given that \(\Delta OAB\) is an equilateral triangle and all unshaded regions are congruent.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the four unshaded overlap regions (each bounded by two arcs) are shown only in the drawing. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
There are 4 unshaded regions (one where each pair of neighbouring rings overlaps). Each is bounded by two arcs of \(60^\circ\) in circles of radius 7 m, so there are 8 such arcs.

Length of one arc \(= \dfrac{60}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = \dfrac{22}{3}\) m.

Rope needed \(= 8 \times \dfrac{22}{3} = \dfrac{176}{3}\) m, about 58.67 m.

The distance of first pole from base point is 200 m and subsequent poles are installed at equal interval of 150 m. Further, the distance of last pole from the top is 300 m.

Based on above information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a drawing of cable cars hanging from poles; every distance is in the passage. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
The distances of the poles from the base form an AP: 200, 350, 500, ..., with \(a = 200\) and \(d = 150\).

rows.stem: Find the time taken by cable car to reach \(15^{\text{th}}\) pole from the top if it is moving at the speed of 5m/sec and coming from top.
rows.context:
Cable cars at hill stations are one of the major tourist attractions. On a hill station, the length of cable car ride from base point to top most point on the hill is 5000 m. Poles are installed at equal intervals on the way to provide support to the cables on which car moves.

The distance of first pole from base point is 200 m and subsequent poles are installed at equal interval of 150 m. Further, the distance of last pole from the top is 300 m.

Based on above information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression :
rows.solution:
Counted from the top, the first pole is 300 m away and the poles follow every 150 m, so the 15th pole from the top is

\(300 + 14 \times 150 = 2400\) m from the top.

Time \(= \dfrac{2400}{5} = 480\) s, that is, 8 minutes.

rows.stem: Find the total number of poles installed along the entire journey.
rows.context:
Cable cars at hill stations are one of the major tourist attractions. On a hill station, the length of cable car ride from base point to top most point on the hill is 5000 m. Poles are installed at equal intervals on the way to provide support to the cables on which car moves.

The distance of first pole from base point is 200 m and subsequent poles are installed at equal interval of 150 m. Further, the distance of last pole from the top is 300 m.

Based on above information, answer the following questions using Arithmetic Progression :
rows.solution:
The last pole is \(5000 - 300 = 4700\) m from the base, so \(a_n = 4700\):

\(200 + (n - 1) \times 150 = 4700\), so \(n - 1 = 30\) and \(n = 31\).

31 poles are installed.

rows.stem: Represent the above situation with the help of a diagram.
rows.context:
A drone was used to facilitate movement of an ambulance on the straight highway to a point P on the ground where there was an accident.

The ambulance was travelling at the speed of 60 km/h. The drone stopped at a point Q, 100 m vertically above the point P. The angle of depression of the ambulance was found to be \(30^\circ\) at a particular instant.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a picture of the drone at Q above the accident at P with the ambulance on the highway; the passage states every value, and drawing the diagram is the student's task in this part. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Draw the drone at Q, vertically above P with \(QP = 100\) m, and the ambulance at R on the highway through P. Join QR, and draw a horizontal line QS through Q.

The angle of depression \(\angle SQR = 30^\circ\), and it equals the alternate angle \(\angle QRP = 30^\circ\). Triangle QPR is right-angled at P.

rows.stem: Find the distance between the ambulance and the site of accident (P) at the particular instant. (Use \(\sqrt{3} = 1.73\))
rows.context:
A drone was used to facilitate movement of an ambulance on the straight highway to a point P on the ground where there was an accident.

The ambulance was travelling at the speed of 60 km/h. The drone stopped at a point Q, 100 m vertically above the point P. The angle of depression of the ambulance was found to be \(30^\circ\) at a particular instant.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
In right triangle QPR: \(\dfrac{QP}{PR} = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

\(PR = 100\sqrt{3} = 100 \times 1.73 = 173\) m.

rows.stem: Find the time (in seconds) in which the angle of depression changes from \(30^\circ\) to \(45^\circ\).
rows.context:
A drone was used to facilitate movement of an ambulance on the straight highway to a point P on the ground where there was an accident.

The ambulance was travelling at the speed of 60 km/h. The drone stopped at a point Q, 100 m vertically above the point P. The angle of depression of the ambulance was found to be \(30^\circ\) at a particular instant.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Let M be the point on PR where the angle of depression is \(45^\circ\). In right triangle QPM, \(\dfrac{QP}{PM} = \tan 45^\circ = 1\), so \(PM = 100\) m.

The ambulance covers \(MR = 173 - 100 = 73\) m.

Speed \(= 60\) km/h \(= 60 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = \dfrac{50}{3}\) m/s.

Time \(= 73 \times \dfrac{3}{50} = \dfrac{219}{50} \approx 4.4\) s.

rows.stem: How long (in seconds) will the ambulance take to reach point P from a point T on the highway such that angle of depression of the ambulance at T is \(60^\circ\) from the drone ?
rows.context:
A drone was used to facilitate movement of an ambulance on the straight highway to a point P on the ground where there was an accident.

The ambulance was travelling at the speed of 60 km/h. The drone stopped at a point Q, 100 m vertically above the point P. The angle of depression of the ambulance was found to be \(30^\circ\) at a particular instant.

Based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
In right triangle QPT, \(\dfrac{QP}{PT} = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\), so \(PT = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{3}}{3}\) m.

Time \(= \dfrac{100\sqrt{3}}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{50} = 2\sqrt{3} \approx 3.5\) s.
